title: "Filtering and Selecting"
---

# Filtering and Selecting

These adaptors decide which items come out, and sometimes how many. They are lazy. `filter` does not build a smaller `Vec` until you collect.

## The concept

`filter` keeps items for which the predicate returns `true`. `filter_map` combines a test and a transform by returning `Option`. `take` and `skip` count items. `take_while` and `skip_while` look at values. `step_by` keeps every nth item.

`take_while` and `skip_while` consume the first element that fails the predicate. That element is not yielded, and you do not get it back from the same iterator.

## Recipe 18 — Keeping elements that match a condition with filter()

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [18, 21, 19, 30, 12];
    let hot: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().filter(|n| *n >= 20).collect();
    assert_eq!(hot, [21, 30]);
}
```

The predicate is `FnMut(&Item)`. It may update its own captured state. It should not have a side effect you depend on for items you later `take` past, because those items never reach the predicate if an earlier adaptor stops the pull. The predicate does run for every item `filter` pulls.

## Recipe 19 — Filtering and transforming in one step with filter_map()

Return `None` to drop the item. Return `Some(value)` to yield `value`, which may be a different type.

```rust
fn main() {
    let raw = ["18", "nope", "21", ""];
    let readings: Vec<i32> = raw.iter().filter_map(|text| text.parse().ok()).collect();
    assert_eq!(readings, [18, 21]);
}
```

`parse` returns `Result`. `.ok()` turns `Err` into `None`, which `filter_map` drops. The error message is discarded. If you need that message, collect into `Result` instead of using `filter_map`. This recipe is the "skip bad rows" tool, not the "report bad rows" tool.

## Recipe 20 — Taking the first N elements with take() and take_while()

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [5, 8, 11, 3, 20];
    let prefix: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().take(3).collect();
    assert_eq!(prefix, [5, 8, 11]);

    let rising: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().take_while(|n| *n < 10).collect();
    assert_eq!(rising, [5, 8]);
}
```

`take_while` stops at `11` and does not look at `3` or `20`. `11` itself is consumed and dropped. It is not in `rising`, and it is not available as the next item of this same iterator.

`take(0)` yields nothing. `take` on an infinite iterator is the usual way to make it finite.

## Recipe 21 — Skipping elements with skip() and skip_while()

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [0, 0, 4, 5, 0];
    let after_header: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().skip(2).collect();
    assert_eq!(after_header, [4, 5, 0]);

    let after_zeros: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().skip_while(|n| *n == 0).collect();
    assert_eq!(after_zeros, [4, 5, 0]);
}
```

`skip(2)` drops two items by count. `skip_while` drops a prefix of zeros and then yields everything else, including a later zero. It does not mean "drop every zero".

## Recipe 22 — Sampling every Nth element with step_by()

`step_by(n)` yields the first item, then skips `n - 1`, and repeats. `step_by(0)` panics.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15];
    let sampled: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().step_by(2).collect();
    assert_eq!(sampled, [10, 12, 14]);

    let odd_indexes: Vec<_> = readings.into_iter().skip(1).step_by(2).collect();
    assert_eq!(odd_indexes, [11, 13, 15]);
}
```

`skip(1).step_by(2)` is how you start on the second element. `step_by` always keeps its first remaining item.
